_meta.descricao: The monograms, symbols, vestments, and liturgical objects that make up the visual language of the Catholic faith through the centuries.
_meta.aviso: An initial set of the most recognizable symbols; it does not exhaust the richness of all Catholic sacred iconography.

itens.resumo: The cross bearing the body of Christ, the central symbol of the Catholic faith, required by liturgical norm beside every altar of celebration.
itens.corpo:
The crucifix — the cross with the image of the body of the crucified Christ — visually condenses the core of the Christian faith: the Passion and Death of Jesus as the supreme act of redeeming love. It differs from the bare cross (more frequent in Protestant contexts, which tend to emphasize the Resurrection) by keeping the Crucified One visible. Its doctrinal legitimacy goes back to the Second Council of Nicaea (787), the seventh ecumenical council, which, bringing the iconoclast crisis to an end, reaffirmed the veneration of sacred images and distinguished adoration (latria), due to God alone, from the veneration (dulia) given to images — the honor of which passes to the one represented in them. The decisive argument was Christological: because the Word became man and had a visible face, it is lawful to depict him.

In Catholic liturgical discipline, the crucifix is required beside the altar. The General Instruction of the Roman Missal (third typical edition, 2002), no. 308, states: "There is also to be a Cross, with the figure of Christ crucified upon it, either on the altar or near it, where it is clearly visible to the assembled congregation. It is fitting that such a cross, which calls to mind for the faithful the saving Passion of the Lord, remain near the altar even outside of liturgical celebrations." The norm, therefore, does not merely ask for a cross, but for a cross with the effigie Christi crucifixi — the body of the Crucified One — clearly visible to the assembly.

The presence of the crucifix in public spaces has been the subject of recent legal dispute. In the case of Lautsi v. Italy, the Second Section of the European Court of Human Rights ruled on 3 November 2009, unanimously, that the compulsory display of the crucifix in Italian state classrooms violated religious freedom and the right to education. The decision provoked an unprecedented reaction: ten member states of the Council of Europe intervened in the case in support of Italy, and the Italian government appealed to the Grand Chamber, which on 18 March 2011 overturned the judgment by 15 votes to 2, holding that the decision to perpetuate a tradition falls within the national margin of appreciation and that "a crucifix on a wall is an essentially passive symbol," whose influence on pupils cannot be compared to that of didactic speech.

As a work of art, one of the most famous crucifixes is Cimabue's for the Basilica of Santa Croce in Florence, painted in tempera on wood around 1265 (about 4.5 meters high), commissioned by the Franciscan friars and one of the first Italian works to break with the late Byzantine style through its more corporeal representation of Christ. It survived the flooding of the Arno River on 4 November 1966, which tore away a good part of the painted surface — the loss of about 60% of the original paint is estimated — and underwent a ten-year restoration led by Umberto Baldini and Ornella Casazza, using a method that chose not to disguise the lacunae. Its submerged photograph became one of the emblematic images of the artistic catastrophe of Florence.

Beyond liturgical use, the crucifix remains one of the most immediate identifying signs of the Catholic presence in homes, schools and public space, and a recurring object of debates on the secular nature of the State and religious freedom.

itens.resumo: The trigram formed by the first three letters of the name of Jesus in Greek, spread by Saint Bernardine of Siena and adopted as the emblem of the Society of Jesus.
itens.corpo:
IHS derives from the first three letters of the name "Jesus" in Greek (ΙΗΣΟΥΣ — Iota, Eta, Sigma), transliterated into the Latin alphabet (IHS or JHS). It is one of the forms of the Western christogram, the monogram that abbreviates the name of Christ. Devotion to the Holy Name developed above all from the 12th and 13th centuries onward, with roots in authors such as Saint Anselm of Canterbury († 1109) and Saint Bernard of Clairvaux († 1153); Saint Francis of Assisi, in his Testament, already recommended gathering up and keeping in a worthy place the names of the Lord written in unsuitable places.

The great propagator of the trigram was the Franciscan Saint Bernardine of Siena (1380–1444), one of the most famous preachers of 15th-century Italy, who traveled throughout the peninsula preaching the Name of Jesus as an instrument of reconciliation between families and rival factions (Guelphs and Ghibellines). To give visual effectiveness to the message, Bernardine used to preach holding a wooden tablet with the monogram painted in golden Gothic letters, which he enriched with a cross over the letter H (or tau), alluding to the Passion, and with a blazing sun of twelve wavy rays around the letters, referring to the Resurrection. The practice caused controversy: around 1427 he was accused of idolatry and of a dangerous novelty by certain Dominican and Augustinian theologians, who feared that the people would worship the physical tablet as an amulet, and he was summoned to appear in Rome before Pope Martin V. In the public controversy, with the support of his disciple Saint John of Capistrano, the orthodoxy of the devotion was recognized; the pope approved it in 1427 and asked that the cross be included in the monogram, followed by a solemn procession through the streets of Rome. Later, in 1455, Pope Callixtus III asked Saint John of Capistrano to preach a crusade invoking the Most Holy Name against the Ottoman Turks, whose defeat before Belgrade in 1456 was attributed to this invocation.

The spread of the IHS was not limited to devotional use: the monogram, set against a radiant sun, was used in 15th-century Italy to replace, in public spaces, both pagan symbols and the emblems of political factions. The feast of the Most Holy Name of Jesus, celebrated at first locally, was extended to the whole Catholic Church by Pope Innocent XIII on December 20, 1721, at the request of Emperor Charles VI of Germany, and was then fixed on the second Sunday after the Epiphany; the reform of Pius X (motu proprio Abhinc duos annos, 1913) moved it to the Sunday between January 2 and 5, and John Paul II reinstituted it on January 3. In 1530 Clement VII had ordered the Franciscans to adopt the office of the Most Holy Name, with the hymn "Iesu decus angelicum". In 1862 Pius IX approved the Litany of the Most Holy Name of Jesus, later endorsed by Leo XIII for the whole Church.

Subsequently, the IHS was adopted as the official emblem of the Society of Jesus: Saint Ignatius of Loyola took the monogram as his seal when he was elected first Superior General in 1541, and thus it became the emblem of the institute; its Jesuit form shows the H surmounted by a cross, above three nails (an allusion to the nails of the Passion) and surrounded by a sun. The motif appears carved on church facades — as on that of the Gesù in Rome, where it crowns the high altar, and on the ceiling of the nave, in Baciccio's "Apotheosis of the Name of Jesus" (1676–79) —, embroidered on vestments and engraved on sacred vessels, tombstones and objects of devotion. The popular — not etymological — reading of the trigram as an acronym of the Latin phrase "Iesus Hominum Salvator" ("Jesus, Savior of Men") became established through use, even though its origin is the Greek letters of the name itself.

itens.resumo: The first two Greek letters of the word "Christ" superimposed, one of the oldest Christian symbols, associated with Constantine's victory at the Milvian Bridge.
itens.corpo:
The Chrismon, or Chi-Rho, superimposes the Greek letters Chi (Χ) and Rho (Ρ), the first two of the word ΧΡΙΣΤΟΣ (Christos, "Christ"), in such a way that the vertical stem of the rho crosses the center of the chi. It is one of the oldest forms of the Christogram, attested since Late Antiquity. In the fourth century, according to the account of Lactantius in De Mortibus Persecutorum (c. 315), Constantine saw a sign of light in the form of a cross before facing Maxentius; Bishop Eusebius of Caesarea, in the Life of Constantine (composed after 337), describes a cross of light above the sun accompanied by the Greek words "(ἐν) τούτῳ νίκα" — "by this, conquer" —, which the Latin tradition rendered as the phrase "in hoc signo vinces". The two accounts do not entirely coincide, but tradition united them with the Battle of the Milvian Bridge, fought on October 28, 312, and with the subsequent adoption of the military standard bearing the monogram, the labarum. According to the traditional narrative, Constantine's troops painted the Chi-Rho on their shields before the battle; the victory over Maxentius, who drowned in the collapse of a bridge of boats over the Tiber, opened the way to the Edict of Milan of 313, which granted tolerance to Christians.

One point that is often distorted should be made precise: the phrase "in hoc signo vinces" is a later Latin formula, and not the literal quotation of Eusebius, who records the Greek words. The sign described by Eusebius is, moreover, a Christogram (Chi-Rho, sometimes with Alpha and Omega), whereas Lactantius speaks of a tropaion in the form of a cross. Historians also observe that Eusebius's account is the latest and the most problematic of the three: written after Constantine's death, it does not appear in the De mortibus persecutorum nor in Eusebius's own Ecclesiastical History, and it does not even place the vision on October 27–28, 312 — which leads some scholars to doubt the literalness of the episode. From Constantine onward, the Chi-Rho spread across shields, coins, sarcophagi, catacombs and Christian buildings, and since then it frequently appears flanked by the Alpha and the Omega, the first and last letters of the Greek alphabet, alluding to Christ as beginning and end (Rev 1:8).

The very name "chrismon" is linked to a Milanese tradition: according to Landulf of Milan (twelfth century), Saint Ambrose is said to have used the symbol to introduce catechumens to the mysteries of the faith, and the term "chrismon" (from the Greek chresmos, "oracle") is said to have derived from this, giving rise to the Latin name of the symbol. Corresponding to this tradition is the celebrated marble slab known as the Chrismon Sancti Ambrosii, preserved in the Duomo of Milan, with the Chi-Rho monogram and the Alpha and Omega inscribed in a circle; a Baroque frame, added in 1669, bears the Latin inscription that interprets the symbol: "Circulus hic Summi continet nomina Regis / Quem sine principio et sine fine vides / Principium cum fine tibi denotat Α Ω" — "this circle contains the name of the Most High King, whom you see without beginning and without end; the Alpha and the Omega signify to you the beginning and the end". The Chi-Rho also appears surrounded by a laurel wreath on the fourth-century sarcophagus attributed to the Domitilla family, in Rome, where the garland symbolizes the victory of the Resurrection over death.

In the book arts, the Chi-Rho was widely used: the page of the famous Book of Kells (folio 34r) opens the account of the Nativity with a richly ornamented Chi-Rho initial. The symbol remains alive in contemporary sacred art, engraved on chalices, liturgical furnishings, pediments and mosaics, and serves as the emblem of ecclesiastical and educational institutions.

itens.resumo: The two extreme letters of the Greek alphabet, a symbol of Christ as the beginning and end of all creation, and one of the earliest visual confessions of the divinity of Christ in Christian art.
itens.corpo:
"I am the Alpha and the Omega, the beginning and the end, says the Lord God" (Rev 1:8; cf. 21:6 and 22:13) — the two extreme letters of the Greek alphabet, placed side by side, became a direct symbol of this self-declaration of Christ as the origin and destiny of all history and of all creation. The title appears three times in the Book of Revelation, and the distribution is not accidental: in chapter 1 it is applied to God, "who is, and who was, and who is to come, the Almighty"; in the last two chapters, to Christ. For a good number of exegetes, this is one of the indications that the author attributes to Christ the very divinity of God. Textual criticism also records that Rev 1:11, in some later versions, repeats "I am the Alpha and the Omega," but this phrase does not appear in the oldest manuscripts, such as Codex Alexandrinus, Codex Sinaiticus, and Codex Ephraemi Rescriptus. The Greek formula replaces the Hebrew "first and last" already used in Isaiah (Is 41:4; 44:6; 48:12) and repeated in the Book of Revelation itself (Rev 1:17-18; 2:8); in the Greek text, the Alpha and the Omega comes to take the place of the Hebrew תא (from aleph to tav) as an expression of totality.

The Christian interpretation of the symbol is attested very early. Clement of Alexandria (d. c. 215) calls the Word "Alpha and Omega, he by whom alone the end becomes a beginning and again ends in the original beginning without any interruption" (Stromata IV,25). Tertullian, in De Monogamia (v), also refers to Christ with this title. In the fourth century, the poet Prudentius sums up the common reading in the verses of the Cathemerinon (hymn IX, 10-12): "Alpha et Omega cognominatus, ipse fons et clausula omnium quae sunt, fuerunt, quaeque post futura sunt" — that is, the very beginning and the very close of all that is, was, and will be.

It was, however, in the monuments of early Christendom that the Alpha and the Omega enjoyed their widest diffusion. The earliest date on which the symbol occurs is 295, in a dated inscription from Rome, in which the Omega appears preceding the Alpha and both letters form part of the epigraphic text itself. In a fresco from the middle of the fourth century, in the "great cave" of the Catacomb of Praetextatus, Alpha and Omega appear joined to the monogrammatic cross; the earliest inscription in which the letters appear in the traditional form dates from 364. From then on they became a favorite symbol of orthodox Christians — the Arians, precisely because they denied the full divinity of the Son, looked on the symbol with disfavor, which makes it a kind of anti-Arian watchword. The letters were represented in three ways: alone; in connection with human figures; or combined with other symbols, such as the cross and the Chi-Rho (Christogram). On the stone tablet in the Catacomb of Domitilla, in Rome, for example, the Chi-Rho is flanked by the Alpha and the Omega.

In liturgical use, the formula became fixed above all in the Paschal Candle. At the Easter Vigil, after the blessing of the new fire, the priest cuts a cross into the candle, then the numerals of the current year and the Greek letters Alpha and Omega, proclaiming: "Christ yesterday and today, the Beginning and the End, the Alpha and the Omega. His are the times and the ages." The gesture inscribes Christ's Passover in human time and proclaims him Lord of history — just as the letters, also engraved on tombstones, sealed the hope of the resurrection of the faithful.

itens.resumo: One of the oldest symbols of Christianity, a Greek acrostic that professes faith in Christ the Son of God and Savior, linked from early on to the Eucharist and Baptism.
itens.corpo:
The Greek word "ichthys" (ἸΧΘΥΣ, fish) is an acrostic: each of its five letters begins a word of the confession of faith "Iesous Christos Theou Yios Soter" (Ἰησοῦς Χριστός, Θεοῦ Υἱός, Σωτήρ) — "Jesus Christ, Son of God, Savior." The symbol is attested from the second century in both textual and archaeological sources. The oldest literary reference to the fish as a Christian sign is found in Clement of Alexandria (born c. 150), who, in the Paedagogus (III, 11), recommends that his readers have a dove or a fish engraved on their rings and seals — without considering any explanation necessary, a sign that the meaning of the symbol was already familiar. Tertullian, at the beginning of the third century, applies it to the faithful: "we, little fishes, after the example of our Ichthys, Jesus Christ, are born in water" (De baptismo, 1). Saint Augustine, in the City of God (XVIII), explains that the initial letters of the five Greek words form the word "fish," under which Christ is mystically understood, citing the passage as a prophecy of the Erythraean Sibyl.

Two epigraphic witnesses give the symbol its Eucharistic dimension. The inscription of Abercius, bishop of Hieropolis in Phrygia (end of the 2nd century / beginning of the 3rd, traditionally dated c. 216), describes the bishop's journeys from his Asian homeland to Rome — the "queen in golden garments" — and his travels with Paul as his companion; as food, he says he received the "fish from the spring, the great, the pure," together with bread and wine mixed with water: Eucharistic symbols par excellence. The original fragments were recovered by William Ramsay in 1883, reused in a wall of the baths of Hieropolis, and are now preserved in the Vatican Museums (there is a cast in the Museo della Civiltà Romana). The inscription of Pectorius, discovered on June 24, 1839 in the cemetery of Saint-Pierre-l'Estrier, in Autun (France), was carved in Greek, in verse, on a marble tablet recovered in fragments; the text celebrates the fish as spiritual food and speaks of "holding the fish in one's hands," a formula that scholars have debated because it suggests, besides the bread and wine, a third element. Its dating, deduced from style, symbolism, and paleography, points to the end of the second century or the beginning of the third.

In the Roman catacombs the fish appears among the principal Christian symbols: in Eucharistic scenes, the food before the banqueters is invariably bread and fish on separate plates, as in the famous scene of the Fractio Panis (cemetery of Priscilla) and in the fishes on the grass, beside the baskets of bread and wine, in the crypt of Lucina. Associated with the dove, the anchor, and the monogram of Christ, it appears in frescoes, sculptures, rings, seals, and gold glass from the first to the fourth century; from the second century on, the form of the dolphin is frequent. The fish symbol begins to decline after the fourth century, when its representations come to have a mainly ornamental character, linked to baptismal water. The acrostic thus sums up a brief creed in Christ, God and Savior, and remains one of the oldest and most widespread signs of recognition of Christianity.

itens.resumo: A biblical image that unites the sacrifice of the lamb at the Jewish Passover with the redemptive sacrifice of Christ, the "Agnus Dei," and which the Roman liturgy repeated before communion, to the point of linking it to the rejection of an Eastern council.
itens.corpo:
The image of the Lamb goes back to the paschal lamb slaughtered in Exodus, whose blood, sprinkled on the doorposts of the Hebrew houses, protected them from the tenth plague (Ex 12). The prescription was strict: the flesh had to be eaten that same night and "you shall not break a bone of it" (Ex 12:46; cf. Num 9:12). The figure is taken up by John the Baptist upon seeing Jesus: "Behold, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world" (Jn 1:29), and applied to Christ by Saint Paul — "Christ, our Passover, has been sacrificed" (1 Cor 5:7) — and by Saint Peter, who speaks of the "lamb without blemish" and of the precious blood of redemption (1 Pet 1:19). The Johannine tradition further brings the account of the Passion close to the paschal rite: according to Jn 19:14, when Jesus was sentenced it was the sixth hour of the Preparation Day (noon), the moment at which, in the Temple, the slaughter of the paschal lambs began; and, unlike the two thieves, "they did not break his legs" (Jn 19:33), fulfilling the ancient prescription about the lamb.

The Book of Revelation makes the figure the center of the heavenly liturgy: the Lamb "as though it had been slain" stands before the throne, with seven horns and seven eyes — "which are the seven spirits of God sent out into all the earth" (Rev 5:6) — receiving the adoration of the elders, the living creatures, and the multitudes. Thus the image gathers, in a single symbol, redemptive suffering and paschal victory. It is this slain and victorious Lamb whom the liturgy of the Mass invokes shortly before communion, in the chant "Lamb of God, you take away the sins of the world."

The chant of the Agnus Dei was introduced into the Mass of the Roman rite by Pope Sergius I (687–701). A little-remembered context: its spread in the West occurs in reaction to the Council in Trullo (the Quinisext Council, of 692), whose canons — especially canon 82 — forbade representing Christ under the figure of a lamb, requiring that he be depicted in his human form, as a confession of the reality of the Incarnation. Sergius I did not accept the Trullan canons; the formula of those councils would later be received by Hadrian I and associated with the defense of icons. Curiously, the object of the Eastern prohibition — the lamb — became, in the Latin chant, the very title of Christ.

In sacred art the motif appears above all on altars and in stained-glass windows. The Lamb is usually represented with the cruciform nimbus — a sign of his divine nature and of the sacrifice of the cross — resting upon the book of the seven seals (Rev 5) or holding the banner of the Resurrection (the vexillum, generally white with a red cross), which unites the cross to the paschal victory. A symbol easy for the first Christians to read and deeply rooted in Scripture, it became one of the most constant images of Western sacred art.

itens.resumo: A mistaken naturalist legend, fixed in writing by the Physiologus, about a bird said to feed its young with its own blood became a traditional symbol of Christ's Eucharistic sacrifice, immortalized in the hymn Adoro te devote of Thomas Aquinas.
itens.corpo:
The pelican that wounds its own breast to feed its young with blood is, in sacred art, one of the most enduring visual metaphors of Christ giving himself in the Eucharist. The belief has no zoological basis: it derives from a mistaken observation. To feed its brood, the pelican bends its long bill against its breast in order to regurgitate the fish it has caught, and the blood of the prey stains its feathers red, giving the impression that it is tearing its own flesh. The legend was set down in writing in the Physiologus, a naturalist-theological text composed in Alexandria, Egypt, probably around the year 200, and written for the purpose of Christian edification. In one version, the mother feeds her young with her blood in time of famine; in another, she finds them dead in the nest and revives them with her blood, sacrificing her own life. The author of the Physiologus read the pelican in light of an obscure verse of Psalm 101:7 in the Septuagint ("I have become like a pelican of the wilderness"; Ps 102:6 in the Vulgate), putting on the lips of Christ this expression of messianic solitude and of the Passion.

The metaphor took hold in the patristic tradition. Epiphanius of Salamis read in the pelican a figure of the Resurrection and of the life-giving power of Christ's blood, and Jerome also took up the image, associating it with Christ's loving self-gift. John 19:34 — the pierced side of Christ, from which blood and water flow — provided the most direct scriptural foundation for the comparison: as Augustine observed, the water is for purification and the blood for forgiveness, the Church being born from the open side of Christ, just as Eve was formed from the side of the sleeping Adam. The Physiologus was translated from Greek into Latin between the fourth and the early sixth century and, from there, into Ethiopic, Armenian, Syriac, and a multitude of European and Eastern languages; at the end of the twelfth century, its legends were absorbed by the bestiaries, a genre of natural history book that combined encyclopedic learning with moral interpretation — and thus the pelican entered Gothic stained-glass windows, illuminated manuscripts, altar reliefs, and tabernacles.

The literary high point of the symbol is in the final stanza of the Eucharistic hymn Adoro te devote, attributed to Thomas Aquinas and probably written around 1260: "Pie pelicane, Iesu Domine, me immundum munda tuo sanguine, cuius una stilla salvum facere totum mundum quit ab omni scelere" — "O loving pelican, Lord Jesus, cleanse me, unclean, with your blood, of which one single drop can save the whole world from all sin." Unlike the other hymns composed for the feast of Corpus Christi, instituted by Urban IV in 1264 (such as the Pange lingua and the Lauda Sion), the Adoro te devote was not written for the liturgy and does not appear in liturgical texts of the period; some scholars suppose that the friar wrote it for private use during Mass. It was only incorporated into the Roman Missal in 1570. The pelican stanza, designated by its opening words "Jesu pie pelicane" or "Pie pelicane," is sometimes used on its own as a hymn at Benediction of the Blessed Sacrament.

The pelican also appears in the poetry of Dante Alighieri, who in the Paradiso (canto XXV) calls Christ "nostro Pelicano," and in figurative art it is above all in scenes of the Crucifixion that the bird is usually depicted, among the many species of the bestiary. In English, this type of image is called "pelican in her piety" or "vulning pelican," from the Latin vulnerare, "to wound," precisely because the bird wounds itself to give life. Thus, a poorly understood zoological observation was transformed, over more than a millennium, into a silent profession of faith in the real presence of Christ in the Eucharist.

itens.resumo: The geometric figure with three equal sides and a single outline as a visual symbol of the unity and equality of the three divine Persons, and the medieval diagram of the "Shield of the Faith" (Scutum Fidei) with its twelve "is / is not" propositions.
itens.corpo:
The equilateral triangle—three identical sides and three identical angles forming a single closed figure—became a recurring, though necessarily limited, visual symbol of Trinitarian doctrine: three truly distinct Persons (Father, Son and Holy Spirit) and, at the same time, one and the same God, with no subordination of one Person to the others. By its very geometry, it expresses the equality of the Persons and the unity of the divine essence, and for this reason it appears in altarpieces, stained-glass windows, pediments and ceilings of churches dedicated to the Most Holy Trinity. It is, like every image applied to the mystery, an imperfect analogy: no figure can exhaust the inner life of God.

The most elaborate form of this symbol is the so-called Shield of the Trinity or Scutum Fidei ("shield of faith," an expression taken from Eph 6:16 in the Vulgate). It is a diagram of four circular nodes joined by six links: the three outer nodes bear the names of the Persons (PATER, FILIUS, SPIRITUS SANCTUS) and the central node, Deus or DEUS; the lines affirm "is" (est) between each Person and God, and "is not" (non est) between the Persons themselves—"the Father is not the Son," "the Son is not the Holy Spirit," "the Holy Spirit is not the Father." The whole sums up, in twelve propositions, the first part of the Athanasian Creed ("The Father is God, the Son is God, the Holy Spirit is God; and yet they are not three Gods, but one God").

The diagram is attested from a manuscript of c. 1208–1216 of the Compendium Historiae in Genealogia Christi by Peter of Poitiers, and was popularized in the Summa de Vitiis (c. 1250) of the Dominican William Peraldus, connected with moral instruction. Its use spread widely in the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries, in English and French manuscripts and books (such as the Sherborne Missal), in stained glass and carvings in churches (many in the region of East Anglia) and in heraldry: in the Wernigerode Armorial (southern Germany, c. 1486–1492) the Scutum Fidei appears as the "coat of arms of God," with helm, crown and the dove of the Holy Spirit as the crest. The name "Shield of the Trinity," today the most common, only came into regular use in the twentieth century; in the Middle Ages Scutum Fidei prevailed.

A symbol often associated with this one is the Eye of Providence—an eye inscribed in a triangle or surrounded by rays of glory, representing the omniscience and care of God. Its origin is Renaissance and Christian: an early example is the Supper at Emmaus by Jacopo Pontormo (1525), in which the eye in a triangle was added, it is supposed, to replace a three-faced symbol of the Trinity that the Counter-Reformation had prohibited; the motif also appears in Cesare Ripa's Iconologia (1593). Only in the eighteenth century, about two centuries later, was the Eye of Providence appropriated by Freemasonry as an emblem of the "Great Architect of the Universe." It is therefore worth distinguishing carefully: the Trinitarian triangle and the Scutum Fidei are medieval Christian doctrinal symbols, and the Eye of Providence is a Renaissance Christian image that only later received profane uses.

itens.titulo: The Dove of the Holy Spirit
itens.resumo: The biblical image that represents the third Person of the Trinity descending upon Jesus at His Baptism and upon the Church at Pentecost, and which became the center of Bernini's stained-glass window of the Cathedra Petri in Saint Peter's Basilica.
itens.corpo:
The white dove in flight, usually radiating rays of light, is the most universal visual representation of the Holy Spirit in Christian art, based directly on the Gospel accounts of the Baptism of Jesus: "the Holy Spirit descended upon him in bodily form as a dove" (Lk 3:22; cf. Mt 3:16 and Jn 1:32). The episode is the iconographic model that Christian art developed in scenes of the Annunciation, Baptism, Transfiguration and Pentecost (Acts 2), where the dove sometimes crowns tongues of fire. The Fathers saw in the dove signs of purity, gentleness and peace, associating it with the bird sent out by Noah that returned with an olive branch (Gen 8:11), a sign of reconciliation, and relating it to the Spirit who hovers over the waters in Gen 1:2. In the Roman catacombs the dove appears frequently, there also read as a symbol of the soul that has attained divine peace.

The most famous example in sacred art is the stained-glass window that dominates the apse of Saint Peter's Basilica in the Vatican, in the ensemble known as the Cathedra Petri (Chair of Peter). It is a work by Gian Lorenzo Bernini commissioned by Pope Alexander VII (r. 1655-1667). The gilded bronze reliquary, which encloses the ancient wooden chair attributed to Peter, was solemnly placed above the altar on January 17, 1666. It is noteworthy that the examination of the relic carried out by the archaeologist Giovanni Battista De Rossi in 1867 — the last time the chair was displayed — concluded that only the acacia wood frame dates back to Antiquity, while the other parts of oak and the ivory plaques are the result of a reconstruction from the Byzantine era, and that it is not the chair personally used by the Apostle.

The ensemble is supported by four colossal statues of about five meters, in gilded bronze, representing the Doctors of the Church: the two outer figures, slightly larger, are the Latin Doctors Ambrose and Augustine; the two inner ones, the Greek Doctors Athanasius and John Chrysostom. Above the chair, among golden clouds and angels flying amid rays of light, opens the Bohemian glass window, divided into twelve sections in honor of the twelve Apostles who carried the Gospel throughout the world; against it stands out the dove, symbol of the Holy Spirit, described as the soul of the Church whom He never ceases to help and guide. The light that passes through the window — of translucent alabaster and glass — casts a golden brightness into the basilica, more intense in the afternoon. In Saint Peter's Basilica, the dove of the Holy Spirit, placed above the chair of the successor of Peter, visually unites the Spirit's assistance to the Church and the Petrine ministry.

itens.resumo: The image of the heart of Christ, crowned with thorns, wounded, and aflame with love, the central symbol of the devotion of reparation spread from the revelations to Saint Margaret Mary Alacoque at Paray-le-Monial.
itens.corpo:
The representation of the Sacred Heart of Jesus — a visible heart, crowned with thorns, pierced by a lance, wrapped in flames and often surmounted by a cross — took shape from the private revelations that Saint Margaret Mary Alacoque (1647–1690), a religious of the Visitation, claimed to have received at Paray-le-Monial, in Burgundy, between 1673 and 1675. According to her Autobiography, in the first of these experiences, on December 27, 1673, Jesus made her rest upon his breast and showed her his heart burning with love; in the second apparition, the following year, specific practices were indicated to her, such as Communion on the first Fridays of the month and the Holy Hour of Eucharistic adoration on Thursday nights, in memory of the agony in Gethsemane; finally, on the feast of the Most Holy Sacrament in 1675, the explicit request is said to have come for a feast in honor of his Heart, to be celebrated on the Friday after the octave of Corpus Christi, accompanied by an act of consecration in reparation. From this message derive the so-called "twelve promises" attributed to the devotion.

The spread of the devotion owes much to the Jesuit Saint Claude de la Colombière (1641–1682), superior of the house of the Society of Jesus in Paray-le-Monial and confessor of the religious, who welcomed and defended the authenticity of her experiences in a context of distrust within the convent itself. Having arrived in Paray in 1675, La Colombière subjected the religious to careful discernment before recognizing her as a soul visited by grace, and advised her to write down her experiences; his testimony helped to establish the devotion, and the Visitation community celebrated the first feast of the Sacred Heart there. Sent afterward as a preacher to England, he interested the Duchess of York in the devotion. Margaret Mary was beatified in 1864 and canonized by Benedict XV on May 13, 1920; La Colombière was beatified by Pius XI in 1929 and canonized by John Paul II on May 31, 1992. The priory church of Paray-le-Monial, raised to the rank of minor basilica by Pius IX in 1875, became one of the great shrines of the devotion in the world.

Ecclesiastical reception was gradual and cautious. The liturgical cult of the Heart of Christ derives, in part, from medieval feasts that included it within the mystery of the Passion and the Holy Wounds, and it had in Saint John Eudes (1601–1680) a forerunner in the seventeenth century: Leo XIII went so far as to say, in 1903, that it was he who introduced the cult of the Sacred Heart of Jesus and of the Heart of Mary, and the decree of beatification declared him "the first who, by divine inspiration, paid them liturgical worship" — the first feast was celebrated on August 31, 1670, in the seminary of Rennes, and Clement X published six bulls granting indulgences to the confraternities of the Sacred Hearts. The devotion nevertheless faced strong Jansenist opposition: Bishop Scipione de' Ricci of Pistoia wrote a pastoral letter against it, and Portuguese and French Jansenism openly opposed it. The proper feast was approved by Clement XIII in 1765, initially granted to Poland and to the Roman Archconfraternity of the Sacred Heart (founded in 1729). The same climate of controversy led Pius VI to condemn, in the bull Auctorem fidei (August 28, 1794), 85 propositions of the Jansenizing Synod of Pistoia (1786), among them the one that unduly restricted adoration of the humanity of Christ (proposition 63) — a text that Pope Francis would cite again in the encyclical Dilexit nos (October 24, 2024). Pius IX extended the feast to the universal Church in 1856. In 1899, in the encyclical Annum Sacrum, Leo XIII solemnly consecrated the entire human race to the Sacred Heart.

From the standpoint of sacred art, the iconographic type of the isolated heart — outside the chest, flaming, girded with thorns and crowned by the cross — spread widely from the nineteenth century onward, when the devotion of reparation spread across Europe and the missions. It is one of the most widely reproduced devotional images in Catholic homes, present in paintings, engravings, holy cards, stained-glass windows and in the very architecture of churches. The very emblem of the Visitation — a heart surmounted by a cross, girded with thorns and pierced by arrows, with the names of Jesus and Mary engraved — links the devotion to the spiritual roots of the order founded by Saint Francis de Sales and Saint Jane de Chantal, which was established in Paray-le-Monial in 1626.

itens.resumo: The band of cloth worn around the neck of the priest or deacon, the distinctive sign par excellence of the authority and the ordained sacramental office.
itens.corpo:
The stole is a long band of cloth worn around the neck by the ordained clergy—crossed over the chest by the priest in the oldest form of the Latin rite, hanging straight in current usage, and worn only over the left shoulder, diagonally, by the deacon. Among all the liturgical vestments, it is the most immediate sign of the office of the one who wears it: the priest does not celebrate Mass or administer the sacraments without it. The Roman Pontifical establishes that, at the ordination of a priest, after the prayer of consecration one of the priests present places the stole on the ordinand "in the manner of a priest" and vests him with the chasuble, while to the deacon the diaconal stole and the dalmatic are given immediately after the prayer of ordination—gestures that outwardly manifest the ministry then conferred.

Its original name was orarium, a term associated with the Latin verb orare (to speak, to preach), which made the band an insignia of preachers; the now-abandoned hypothesis that it derived from the Roman civil garment called the stola has been replaced by explanations linked to a liturgical cloth or a clerical neck scarf, with its introduction placed, at the latest, in the fourth century. In the East it appears first as a distinctive mark of the service of deacons, already mentioned in the canons of the Synod of Laodicea (c. 364). In the West it is attested at least since the sixth century, with frequent citation at that point of the Council of Braga (563) and, with greater documentary certainty, the Synod of Toledo (633), which presents it as a vestment of priests and bishops, given in the very rite of ordination. The name stola, of Gaulish origin, entered France and Spain around the ninth century, reached Italy in the tenth century, and, from the thirteenth century on, practically supplanted the term orarium. The Council of Mainz (813) went so far as to prescribe that "priests always wear the orarium or the stole," and Saint Thomas Aquinas, in the Summa Theologiae, explains the symbolism of the difference in use: the stole represents the yoke of the ministry received; the deacon wears it over the left shoulder, a sign that he acts as an assistant and in dependence on the bishop, while the priest wears it hanging from both shoulders, a sign that he possesses the fullness of sacramental power.

In the Eastern Church the same vestment is called the epitrachilion and is put on over the head, extending down the front; in the Latin Church, the stole must be the color of the day and usually bears a cross that the minister kisses before putting it on. The Roman Missal prescribes its obligatory use for both priests and deacons at Mass. The Council of Trent and later decisions of the Congregation of Rites established stable norms on the form, color, and use of the stole, forbidding it outside the ministries proper to the order. From early on, liturgists underscored its importance: Saint Bruno of Segni (1045–1123) observed that, in order to administer baptism, confirmation, or other functions, the priest may dispense with all the vestments except the stole. For this very reason it is worn—even without the other vestments—in exceptional circumstances, such as confession outside the confessional or the anointing of the sick in an emergency.

itens.resumo: The outermost and most visible vestment of the priest at the celebration of Mass, heir to the Roman cloak, whose form varied from the ample circular cloak to the narrow Roman chasuble and whose color changes according to the liturgical season.
itens.corpo:
The chasuble is the outer liturgical vestment worn by the priest during the celebration of Mass, enveloping the whole body like a sleeveless cloak, placed over the alb and the stole. The General Instruction of the Roman Missal presents it as the vestment proper to the celebrating priest (no. 337), worn over the alb and the stole. Its name comes from the Latin casula, "little house," because it almost entirely enveloped the one who wore it.

Before becoming a liturgical vestment, the chasuble was a common outer garment in the Greco-Latin world: the paenula (in Greek, phainólē), a circular cloak with an opening in the center for the head, sometimes with a hood, which covered the body down to the ankles and protected from cold and rain; the name planeta also derives from it. From the 4th–5th centuries onward, the paenula went out of fashion in civil use, but the Church kept it as the garment of its pastors, perhaps because of its gravity and dignity. By the 6th century it already appears in the mosaics of Ravenna and in documents from the Frankish and Hispanic areas, with use increasingly restricted to the clergy. During the Carolingian period, it became the exclusive vestment of the priest, while Rome had already followed this norm since the 7th century; in the churches of the Eastern rite, the corresponding garment is the phelonion.

Between the 9th and 17th centuries the garment underwent significant modifications. To free the arms, it received progressive lateral cuts, passing from the circular to the ovoid form; then it was shortened in front, taking on a slightly pointed shape. After the Council of Trent, Saint Charles Borromeo tried to curb these cuts in his Instructionum fabricae et supellectilis ecclesiasticae (Milan, 1577), setting dimensions that were still generous: the chasuble — which he also calls phelonium and planeta "because of its width" — was to be about three cubits wide or more, so that, falling from the shoulders, it would form a fold of at least a palm; it was to be of similar length, reaching the heels, with a band at least eight ounces wide sewn from top to bottom, in front and behind, and another transverse band near the top, forming a cross on both sides. Despite this, the process of reduction continued until it transformed the ancient chasuble into something close to a scapular in the shape of a fiddle — the so-called Roman chasuble — with the two panels at times profusely embroidered. In this evolution there is a notable paradox: the more the garment atrophied, the more its ornamentation grew, to the point that the piece became almost more ornament than vestment. In the 19th century the trend was reversed, with the rediscovery of the ancient forms — the Gothic chasuble, ample and flowing, inspired by medieval models — a movement taken up by the liturgical movement, which promoted the renewal of vestments and sacred objects, and consolidated in the post-conciliar period.

The chasuble strictly follows the colors of the liturgical calendar. The General Instruction of the Roman Missal (nos. 345–346) explains that the purpose of the diversity of colors is to express the distinctive character of the mysteries celebrated and the progressive sense of the liturgical year: white or gold on solemnities of the Lord and of non-martyr saints and in the Easter and Christmas seasons; red on Palm Sunday, Good Friday, Pentecost, on feasts of the apostles and evangelists and of martyrs; green in Ordinary Time; violet in Advent and Lent; black, where it is customary, at Masses for the dead; and rose, where it is customary, on Gaudete Sunday (3rd Sunday of Advent) and Laetare Sunday (4th Sunday of Lent). The Gothic and Roman models may be used in both forms of the Roman Rite, and, unless harmony of the whole requires otherwise, it is permitted for concelebrants at the same Mass to use different models.

itens.resumo: The piece of goldsmith's work, also called a custodia, used to expose the consecrated Host for the adoration of the faithful, usually in the radiant form of a sun.
itens.corpo:
The monstrance — also known as the custodia — is a liturgical object of goldsmith's work, usually made of gold, silver or gilded metal, intended to solemnly expose the consecrated Host for the adoration of the faithful, on the altar or in procession. The etymology is straightforward: the word comes from the Latin ostendere, "to show"; the equivalent term monstrance comes from monstrare, with the same meaning. In the first centuries, both names designated any vessel of noble metals fitted with glass or crystal that allowed the contents to be seen — whether the Host or the relic of a saint. Only later did the word become fixed, in Latin usage and in modern languages, for the vessel intended specifically for the Most Blessed Sacrament. The large consecrated Host is fixed in the center of the piece by a small metal clasp called a lunette (from the Latin lunula, "little moon," because of its half-moon shape), fitted behind the transparent crystal.

The object arises historically from the development of the feast and procession of Corpus Christi. The solemnity was promoted by Saint Juliana of Cornillon, a religious of the diocese of Liège, and was instituted for the whole Latin Church by Pope Urban IV through the bull Transiturus de hoc mundo, of August 11, 1264 — in the context of the so-called Eucharistic Miracle of Bolsena, which had occurred shortly before. The need to carry and publicly display the Host in a solemn public procession created the demand for a specific receptacle for this function. According to the Catholic Encyclopedia, inventories of the thirteenth century rarely mention such pieces; at St. Paul's in London there is no reference to a monstrance in 1245 and 1298, but in 1402 a "crystal cross for placing the Body of Christ and carrying it on the feast of Corpus Christi" is already recorded. One of the earliest dated examples usually cited is that of Reims, France, from 1324.

The forms varied greatly over the centuries. The oldest pieces kept the cylindrical crystal shape of the ciborium, mounted on a base and crowned with architectural work, niches and statuettes; later the so-called tower monstrance was adopted, in the form of a small temple or polygonal tower with pinnacles, common from the middle of the fifteenth century. From the second half of the sixteenth century onward, the model that predominates today became widespread: the form of a radiant sun, with rays emanating from the center, frequently adorned, since the eighteenth century, with crowns of angels' heads around the central crystal. Certain examples became monumental: the ark-monstrance of the Cathedral of Genoa (1553) required eight priests to carry it, and the great Spanish custodias could exceed three meters in height, like those of the Cathedral of Toledo, commissioned from Enrique de Arfe in 1515-1523. In the absence of a monstrance, the use of the ciborium for the same purpose is permitted.

The solar form is a theological affirmation before it is an ornament: the rays evoke Christ as the "sun of justice" (Malachi 3:20) and the "light of the world," and the crystal that protects the Host symbolizes purity and the real presence. The Catechism of the Catholic Church, in paragraph 1374, teaches that Christ is present in the Eucharist in a "true, real, and substantial" way. The instruction Redemptionis Sacramentum (Congregation for Divine Worship and the Discipline of the Sacraments, 2004) regulates its use: it is fitting that at the Mass immediately preceding the adoration the Host to be exposed be consecrated and placed in the monstrance on the altar after Communion, and that the exposition be interrupted while Mass is being celebrated. Popular devotion has also preserved the memory of Saint Clare of Assisi, who according to tradition repelled invaders by raising the monstrance with the Most Blessed Sacrament.

itens.resumo: The X-shaped cross (crux decussata), the iconographic attribute of the Apostle Andrew and the national symbol of Scotland under the name of the Saltire.
itens.corpo:
The Cross of Saint Andrew is an X-shaped cross, technically called a crux decussata (from the Latin decussare, "to cut in the shape of an X," a reference to the Roman numeral ten). It is the traditional iconographic attribute of the Apostle Andrew, brother of Peter and, according to tradition, founder of the Church of Byzantium — hence his veneration as patriarch and patron of the Christian East and of the Patriarchate of Constantinople.

There is a historical controversy here that should be recorded clearly. The oldest texts on Andrew's martyrdom — the Acts of Andrew, an apocryphal text of the second century, known to us above all through the compilation of Gregory of Tours — describe him as having been bound, not nailed, to an ordinary Latin cross, and not to an X-shaped cross. The tradition of the X-shaped cross developed later: it is said that Andrew asked for this shape because he considered himself unworthy to die on a cross identical to that of Christ. The familiar iconography that today shows him bound to the X-shaped cross does not seem to have been standardized before the end of the Middle Ages. Tradition places his martyrdom in Patras, in Achaia (Greece), around the year 60.

The association of the X-shaped cross with Scotland has a legendary origin, linked to the Battle of Athelstaneford, traditionally dated to 832, in present-day East Lothian. According to the account, Óengus (Angus) II, king of the Picts, at the head of forces of Picts and Scots, saw in the blue sky the formation of a cloud in the shape of a white saltire — the X of Andrew's martyrdom — and, promising the saint the patronage of Scotland in case of victory, defeated the Angles commanded by Æthelstan. The narrative reaches us through late chroniclers, such as Walter Bower and George Buchanan, and must be treated as legend. Historically, the iconography of the martyrdom on an X-shaped cross appears for the first time in Scotland around 1180, in the reign of William I, and reappears on seals from the end of the thirteenth century, including one of the Guardians of Scotland, from 1286. The Declaration of Arbroath (1320) invokes the conversion of Scotland by Saint Andrew, "the first to be an apostle."

As a symbol, the white saltire on a blue field is, according to tradition, one of the oldest flags in Europe. The oldest textual reference to the Cross of Saint Andrew as a flag is found in the Vienna Book of Hours, c. 1503, where it appears as a white saltire on a red field; the use of the blue field in Scotland goes back at least to the fifteenth century, with the first illustration of a flag in this format in the Register of Scottish Arms, by Sir David Lyndsay of the Mount, c. 1542. The Cross of Saint Andrew is one of the three crosses that make up the flag of the United Kingdom. The same figure, in the form of the Cross of Burgundy, also spread in the heraldry of the Spanish Empire. Outside the national sphere, the X-shaped cross is also called the cross of Saint Thecla and, by association with its related T shape, is sometimes confused in popular devotion with the cross of Saint Anthony.

itens.resumo: The T-shaped letter adopted by Saint Francis of Assisi as his signature and personal symbol, today a hallmark of Franciscan spirituality.
itens.corpo:
The tau cross — also called the cross of Saint Anthony, the cross of Saint Francis, or the Egyptian cross — is a Christian cross in the shape of a T, modeled on the Greek letter tau (τ) and the last letter of the Hebrew alphabet. Its most widespread biblical meaning comes from the Book of Ezekiel: God commands a messenger to mark with a "T" on the forehead those who groan and sigh over the abominations of Jerusalem, so that they may be spared from punishment (Ez 9:3-6). In early Christian antiquity, the shape was already interpreted as a symbol of the cross: the so-called staurogram — a ligature of the letters tau and rho, from the Greek ΣΤΑΥΡΟΣ ("cross") — abbreviated the word "cross" in the oldest manuscripts of the New Testament, such as papyri P66, P45 and P75. The tau was also associated with salvation, whether through identification with the sign in Ezekiel, or through its resemblance to Moses with arms outstretched in Exodus 17:11; Saint Anthony of Egypt already wore it on his mantle.

The Franciscan use of the tau goes back to Francis of Assisi himself, who adopted it as his signature and personal seal, drawing it by hand in his letters and writings. Two direct influences are usually pointed out. The first was the Antonines — a religious community founded in 1095, devoted to caring for lepers, which wore a large tau cross painted on its habit; Francis had close relations with them, since they worked in the leprosarium of Assisi and in the Hospital of Saint Blaise in Rome. The second, and stronger, was the Fourth Council of the Lateran, opened by Pope Innocent III on November 11, 1215. According to the earliest biographers and the Franciscan tradition, Innocent III opened the council with a homily built on Ezekiel 9:4, exhorting the listeners to be marked with the tau; historians generally accept that Francis was present at the assembly. A tradition circulated that the pope concluded by exhorting those present to be "champions of the Tau."

The earliest biographers report that Francis loved and venerated the tau "because it represents the cross and signifies true penance"; he made the sign of the cross with it, preferred it to any other, painted it on the walls of cells, recommended it in preaching, and drew it as his signature in all his letters, "as if his whole concern were to engrave the sign of the tau, according to the prophetic saying, upon the foreheads of men." The theme of penance and continual conversion runs through his writings, such as the Letter to the Faithful (c. 1209-1215), an exhortation about those who do penance and those who do not. As a sign, the tau took on for Francis the meaning of certainty of salvation, of the universality of salvation, and of permanent conversion. In the iconographic tradition, the three knots sometimes depicted on the tau or on the Franciscan cord recall the three religious vows: poverty, obedience and chastity.

After Francis, the tau became established as the distinctive symbol of the Franciscans, on habits, necklaces, chapels and coats of arms, and it remains in use by the Order of Friars Minor and the Secular Franciscan Order, whose members wear it as a pin or medal. The liturgy and popular piety have likewise preserved it as a sign of blessing — Pope Innocent III is said to have used the gesture of the tau to bless — and its association with Ezekiel made it, in eschatological contexts, a sign of election and of protection of the righteous, echoed in the Book of Revelation (7:2-4), where the servants of God are marked on the forehead.

itens.resumo: A central cross potent surrounded by four smaller Greek crosses, linked to the Latin Kingdom of Jerusalem, the Order of the Holy Sepulchre, and devotion to the five wounds.
itens.corpo:
The Jerusalem Cross — also called the five-fold cross, the crusader's cross or, in heraldry, the cross-and-crosslets — is formed by a central cross potent, whose ends terminate in small transverse bars, flanked in the four spaces between its arms by smaller Greek crosses. Its most widespread heraldic version shows the five crosses in gold on a silver field (sometimes on red), the gold-on-silver being one of the rare exceptions allowed to the classical rule of heraldry that forbids metal on metal; it is presumed that the violation was deliberate, because of the special holiness attributed to these arms.

The origin of the design is a matter of debate among scholars. One historiographical tradition associates it with Godfrey of Bouillon, the principal leader of the First Crusade, who is said to have refused the title of king in order to govern Jerusalem as "Defender of the Holy Sepulchre"; this attribution, however, should not be presented as proven fact. The heraldic documentation indicates that the emblem was consolidated only in the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries: the seals of the rulers of Jerusalem in the twelfth century do not show the present design, but a simplified representation of the city, with the Tower of David between the Dome of the Rock and the Holy Sepulchre. The Franciscan friar David Grenier, of the Custody of the Holy Land, maintains that the cross originated in Eastern Christianity, between the fifth and sixth centuries, and was later adopted by the crusaders and by the Kingdom of Jerusalem (1099–1291). In medieval armorials such as the Camden Roll it appears as the arms of the Kingdom of Jerusalem in gold on a silver field. Philip of Courtenay, who held the title of Latin Emperor of Constantinople between 1273 and 1283, used an expanded form in which each of the four crosslets was, in turn, surrounded by four other smaller crosses.

There are several traditional symbolic readings of the five crosses, and they are not mutually exclusive. The most widespread associates them with the five wounds of Christ: the central cross represents the wound in the side opened by the lance, and the four crosslets, the wounds of the hands and feet. Another sees in the four small crosses the four evangelists around Christ, indicating the spread of the Gospel to the four corners of the earth; a third reads the whole as the Old Testament united with the four Gospels.

The cross became the insignia of the Latin Patriarchate of Jerusalem and of the Equestrian Order of the Holy Sepulchre of Jerusalem, a Catholic chivalric institution whose origins go back to the First Crusade and which today maintains works in the Holy Land under the direct protection of the Holy See. It is also the emblem used by the Franciscan Custody of the Holy Land and appears on the national flag of Georgia. Medieval pilgrims tattooed it on their bodies when visiting the Holy Places, a custom still preserved by some Christian families of Jerusalem.

Since the beginning of the twenty-first century, the symbol has come to be appropriated by far-right groups, white supremacists, and Christian nationalists, often associated with the motto "Deus vult." Variants of the cross were displayed, together with the phrase, on flags during the neo-Nazi "Unite the Right" rally in Charlottesville in 2017. In November 2024, a tattoo of the Jerusalem Cross on the chest of Pete Hegseth, then nominee for United States Secretary of Defense, sparked controversy; the Order of the Holy Sepulchre made a public statement clarifying that, for the vast majority of Christians, the cross is a sign of the Passion of Christ and an inspiration to pilgrims, and not a nationalist call.

itens.resumo: The metal staff with a curved tip that the bishop carries, an insignia and sign of his mission as shepherd of the flock entrusted to his care.
itens.corpo:
The pastoral staff (in Latin baculus) is the episcopal insignia that represents the bishop's office as shepherd of the portion of the People of God entrusted to his care, like the staff with which shepherds guide their sheep. Also called the crosier or crozier, it has received various names throughout history — pedum, ferula, cambuta, combula, crocia, virga pastoralis — and in the East it is called the paterissa. As to the origin of the object, the sources differ: some authors trace an affinity with the lituus, the curved rod of the Roman augurs; others consider it an adaptation of the walking sticks used on journeys and, in churches, before the introduction of seats (Catalani, Pont. Rom., Proleg. xx); still others link it to the shepherd's own crook. From a very early date it became one of the principal insignia of the episcopal office.

It is not easy to determine how early it passed into liturgical use. In the earliest texts of the Fathers the word may be taken literally or metaphorically (as in 1 Cor 4:21), and it cannot be established whether it already designates an ecclesiastical ornament. Staffs have been found in the catacombs, dated to the fourth century, but their ceremonial character has not been established. Liturgical use probably goes back to the fifth century, being mentioned in a letter of Pope Celestine I (died 432) to the bishops of Vienne and Narbonne. The first unequivocal reference to it as a liturgical instrument is usually attributed to the Council of Toledo of 633 — the Fourth Council of Toledo, convened by the Visigothic king Sisenand and presided over by Isidore of Seville — although some uncertainty persists about the exact canon in which the mention appears.

Scholars distinguish three ancient forms of the staff. The oldest was a wooden rod bent or curved at the top and pointed at the lower end, known as the pedum. The second had, in place of the curve, a knob often surmounted by a cross, and was called the ferula or cambuta, sometimes used by the popes. The third had at the top a crux decussata, or Greek T, with the arms of the cross sometimes so twisted that they represented two serpents facing each other; this was the crocia, carried by abbots and bishops in the Eastern rite, and from it the present Western form, a shepherd's crook, is derived. The original material was as a rule cypress wood, often covered or inlaid with gold and silver; later, staffs were made of solid ivory, gold, silver and enameled metal. Among the surviving pieces, the staff of Saint Malo, a sixth-century bishop, preserved in the cathedral of Bruges, is cited.

The eleventh and twelfth centuries witnessed a highly elaborate ornamentation of the head of the staff: the handle often ended in a dragon pierced by a cross or in some other allegorical figure, while rich floral decoration filled the curve. In the thirteenth century, the spaces between the spirals received religious themes and statuettes of saints; in Gothic pieces, the knob was set with precious stones. One example is the French crozier from Limoges (c. 1260-1290), in gilt copper and champlevé enamel, whose volute represents the Annunciation and whose knop bears six heraldic shields, with three serpents falling down the shaft.

Liturgically, the bishop carries the staff at solemn pontifical celebrations, by right in his own diocese and by privilege outside it; lesser prelates also use it when they have the privilege of performing pontifical functions. He receives it in the rite of episcopal ordination, when the ordaining bishop pronounces the formula of the Roman Pontifical: «Accipe baculum pastoralis officii; et sis in corrigendis vitiis pie sæviens, judicium sine ira tenens, in fovendis virtutibus auditorum animos mulcens, in tranquillitate severitatis censuram non deserens» — "Receive the staff of the pastoral office; and be piously severe in correcting vices, exercising judgment without anger, soothing the souls of those who hear you by encouraging virtue, and not abandoning, in tranquility, the censure of severity." Tradition interprets each part symbolically: the lower point, sharpened, to goad the indolent; the straight shaft in the middle, to signify just government; and the upper end, curved, to draw in and bring back souls. According to the formulation attributed to Innocent III, the bishop must "spur on the lazy, support the weak, gather the scattered."

The orientation of the volute also distinguished authority: the bishop turned it toward the people over whom his jurisdiction extended, while the abbot turned it backward, indicating that his governance reached only his own community. The abbatial staff is also smaller than the episcopal one and, in the presence of the bishop, is covered with a veil (panniculus). When the bishop is not holding the staff, it is entrusted to a master of ceremonies, the "crosier-bearer," who may wear over his shoulders a shawl-like veil, the vimpa, to hold it without touching it with bare hands. The pope, for his part, does not use the ordinary staff: in ancient depictions he appears with the crosier, but the use disappeared around the eleventh century — Innocent III (d. 1216) attests that it no longer prevailed — and today the pontiff uses the ferula, surmounted by a crucifix. Some symbolists explain the pope's lack of the staff by the legend that Saint Peter handed his staff to a disciple in order to raise a dead man.

itens.resumo: The headdress split into two points, with two hanging bands, worn by bishops and abbots as a sign of their dignity and teaching authority.
itens.corpo:
The mitre (from the Greek μίτρα, "band" or "turban", passing into Latin as mitra) is the liturgical headdress formed by two stiff pieces ending in a point — called cornua — with a band or circle across the forehead and two fringed strips, the lappets or vittae, that fall down the back. It is worn at solemn pontifical celebrations and, in the West, became an insignia not only of bishops, but also of mitred abbots, of cardinals, and of those who are canonically equivalent to a diocesan bishop.

Its origin is Roman: it derives from a non-liturgical headdress distinctive of the pope, the camelaucum, from which the tiara also originates. The camelaucum was already in use at the beginning of the 8th century, as attested by the biography of Pope Constantine I (708–715) in the "Liber Pontificalis"; it is also mentioned in the so-called "Donation of Constantine". The Ordo Romanus IX describes it as made of white material and shaped like a helmet, and the coins of Popes Sergius III (904–911) and Benedict VII (974–983), on which Saint Peter appears wearing the camelaucum, give it the conical form that is the original form of the mitre. The pope wore it above all in solemn processions; in the course of the 10th century he began to wear it also during the liturgical service, and from this the mitre developed.

The first written reference to the mitre is the bull of 1049 of Pope Leo IX — himself formerly Bishop of Toul — who, confirming the primacy of the Church of Trier to its former metropolitan Eberhard, granted him the "Roman mitre" to wear according to the custom of Rome when performing the offices of the church. It is estimated that the mitre was first worn in Rome around the middle of the 10th century and outside Rome by the year 1000; the earliest depictions are in two miniatures from the early 11th century (one in a baptismal register and the other in an Exultet scroll from the cathedral of Bari). Between 1100 and 1150, its use had already become widespread among bishops. During the 11th century the mitre was a conical cap with a band around the forehead; over the course of the 12th century the tip became rounded and then split in the center, forming the two lateral points, until at the end of the 12th century the points came to be placed at the front and back, adorned with a vertical band, the titulus.

In the Latin Church three classes of mitre developed. The mitra pretiosa is richly decorated, sometimes with precious stones and embroidery in gold thread, and was used on the greatest solemnities. The mitra auriphrygiata, in cloth of gold or in white silk with gold and silver threads, was proper to Advent and Lent and to certain parts of the pontifical Mass. The mitra simplex, of white silk damask or linen, without ornament, was used at funerals, at the offices of Good Friday, and when the wearer was not the principal celebrant; at pontifical celebrations two mitres were customarily used, alternated according to the moment.

Among the meanings attributed to its parts, the two points symbolize the knowledge that the prelate must have of the Old and New Testaments, and the two lappets that hang down the back likewise represent the two Testaments. The very pointed shape, raised upward, recalls that the bishop's authority comes from God. The mitre is removed at moments of more direct prayer, such as the Eucharistic Prayer, and, in Catholic ecclesiastical heraldry, since 1969 its use above the personal coat of arms of the clergy has been suppressed, appearing today only in corporate arms, such as those of some dioceses.

itens.resumo: A white wool band in the shape of a "Y", worn by the pope and by metropolitan archbishops as a sign of pastoral ministry and of communion with the See of Rome.
itens.corpo:
The pallium — from the Latin pallium, "woolen cloak" — is a narrow band of white wool placed over the shoulders, on top of the chasuble. Today it has the shape of a "Y", with two pendant strips in front and behind, decorated with six crosses of black silk — one at each end that hangs down over the chest and the back, and four on the ring that rests on the shoulders — and fitted, in front and behind, with three pins (acicula) that recall the three nails of the cross of Christ. The ends are finished with black silk, to recall the dark legs of the lamb that the shepherd carries on his shoulders.

Originally, the pallium was the strip of cloth wrapped around the shoulders worn by all bishops, as seen in the iconography of saints such as Saint Ambrose, Saint Athanasius and Saint John Chrysostom; in early Christian art, Christ and the apostles were depicted with this mantle. It was only from the ninth century onward that it took on its current "Y" shape and became the prerogative of metropolitan archbishops, as a symbol of the jurisdiction they exercise in communion with the Holy See. The first known record of its formal bestowal dates from November 6, 513, when Pope Symmachus gave it to Saint Caesarius of Arles — who, on June 11, 514, would also be named papal vicar for Gaul and Spain.

The making of the pallium preserves a ritual that spans the centuries. Two white lambs, raised by the Trappist monks of the Abbey of Tre Fontane in Rome, are presented and blessed on the memorial of Saint Agnes, on January 21 — the choice of the day is no accident: Agnus, "lamb," echoes the name of the Roman martyr, pierced in the throat as lambs were slaughtered. Since 1644 the animals have been blessed in the Basilica of Saint Agnes Outside the Walls, on the Via Nomentana, and then taken to the pope; one carries white flowers, a symbol of the saint's virginity, and the other red flowers, a symbol of her martyrdom. The wool is then woven and sewn by the cloistered nuns of the Monastery of Saint Cecilia, in Trastevere, and the pallia are kept next to the tomb of Saint Peter, beneath the altar of the Confession, before being bestowed.

The rite of bestowal has undergone recent changes. In 1983, Saint John Paul II instituted the practice of personally placing the pallium on new metropolitan archbishops on the solemnity of Saints Peter and Paul, on June 29. In 2015, Pope Francis changed the custom: he began to bless the pallia in Rome, but entrusted the imposition to the apostolic nuncio in the archdiocese itself, as a sign of the archbishop's bond with the local Church. In June 2025, however, the Office for the Liturgical Celebrations of the Supreme Pontiff announced that Pope Leo XIV would again personally impose the pallia on the feast of the apostles, in Rome — a restoration that took place at the celebration of June 29 of that year, before the new metropolitans.

The Code of Canon Law determines that every metropolitan archbishop must request the pallium from the pope within three months of appointment or consecration, since "the pallium signifies the power which the metropolitan, in communion with the Roman Church, possesses by law in his own province." The sign, therefore, is at once juridical and pastoral: at the Mass for the beginning of his pontificate, on April 24, 2005, Benedict XVI explained that the wool of the lamb represents "the lost sheep, the sick one, the weak one, which the shepherd places on his shoulders and leads to the waters of life."

itens.resumo: The metal vessel suspended from chains in which incense is burned during solemn celebrations, a sign of prayer rising to God.
itens.corpo:
The thurible — from the Latin turibulum, from thus or tus, "incense" — is the vessel in which incense is burned during solemn celebrations. It usually has the shape of a sphere cut in half, in which the burning charcoal and the grains of incense are placed; this base is closed by a movable lid, suspended by chains that are attached to an upper ring. It is handled by the thurifer, assisted by the boat bearer, who carries the boat with the incense to be added during the rite. The name of the minister also comes from the etymology: thurifer, "the one who carries the thurible."

The gesture of incensing has an explicit biblical root. Psalm 141:2 asks that prayer rise like incense into the presence of God, and the Book of Revelation describes an angel at the altar with a golden censer, receiving incense to offer it with the prayers of all the saints (Rev 8:3). Incense also appears among the gifts of the Magi to the Child (Mt 2:11) and in the rites of the Temple of Jerusalem. The Ceremonial of Bishops cites precisely these two texts — Psalm 141 and the Book of Revelation — to ground the use of incense as a sign of reverence and prayer.

The Church distinguishes, with technical precision, the movements of incensation. The ictus is the single swing given to the thurible forward; the ductus is the wider swing, forward and backward. According to the General Instruction of the Roman Missal (no. 277) and the Ceremonial of Bishops itself, the Blessed Sacrament, the relics of the holy Cross and images of the Lord exposed for veneration, the gifts for the sacrifice, the cross of the altar, the Book of the Gospels, the Paschal candle, the celebrating priest, and the people are incensed with three ductus. With two ductus — and only once, after the incensation of the altar — the relics and images of the saints exposed for public veneration are incensed. The incensation of the altar, in turn, is done with simple ictus: all around, when the altar is separated from the wall, or alternately on the right and left sides, when it is against the wall.

The Mass provides for the thurible at various moments: before the entrance procession, before the proclamation of the Gospel, at the offertory and, in the more solemn celebrations, at the consecration, when a deacon puts incense in the thurible and incenses the host and the chalice at each elevation. The number three carries Trinitarian symbolism, a sign of the highest honor; the distinction between three and two ductus serves, in practice, to grade the solemnity according to what is being incensed. It is worth noting that the post-conciliar liturgical books simplified the detailed norms of the Missal of Saint Pius V regarding the number of swings for each person or object, so that certain widespread practices — such as the successive triple of three movements — are not part of the ordinary rite.

itens.resumo: The sign of mockery imposed on Jesus before the crucifixion, transformed by Christian tradition into a symbol of his paradoxical kingship.
itens.corpo:
According to the Gospel accounts, the Roman soldiers wove a crown of thorns and placed it on Jesus' head in the praetorium, ironically hailing him as "King of the Jews" before leading him to Calvary (Mt 27:29; Mk 15:17; Jn 19:2). What began as an instrument of mockery and physical suffering became, in Christian piety and art, one of the most eloquent symbols of the Passion: the kingship of Christ manifested precisely through self-giving and suffering accepted out of love.

The earliest known mention of the crown as a venerated relic was made by Saint Paulinus of Nola, who wrote after 409, referring to it as an object of adoration by the faithful (Letter to Macarius, Patrologia Latina LXI, 407). Cassiodorus, around 570, counted it among the relics that were "the glory" of Jerusalem, and Saint Gregory of Tours claimed that the thorns still appeared green, a freshness miraculously renewed each day. The Breviary of Jerusalem (c. 530) and the itinerary of Antoninus of Piacenza (6th century) indicate that the crown was then displayed in the Basilica on Mount Zion; the pilgrimage of the monk Bernard shows that it remained there in 870. Between the 7th and 10th centuries, however, the relics of Jerusalem were gradually transferred to Constantinople.

It was from Constantinople that the crown passed to the West. In financial crisis, the Latin emperor Baldwin II of Courtenay pledged the relic to Venetian creditors; in 1239, after negotiations, King Louis IX of France paid 135,000 livres tournois, about half of the kingdom's annual revenue, to redeem it and bring it to Paris. Its arrival was celebrated with a procession on August 19, 1239, in which the king himself walked barefoot, without his crown, carrying the relic to Notre-Dame. To house it, Louis IX had the Sainte-Chapelle built, consecrated in 1248, a masterpiece of Rayonnant Gothic conceived as a monumental reliquary. In 1241 other relics of the Passion arrived, among them a fragment of the True Cross.

With the French Revolution, the reliquary was melted down and the crown was transferred for some years to the National Library; restored to the Church after the Concordat of 1801, it was deposited in the Cathedral of Notre-Dame in 1806. In 1896 it received a new circular reliquary of rock crystal, with a rim of worked silver and precious stones. On April 15, 2019, during the fire that devastated Notre-Dame, the relic was safely removed and kept at the Louvre, returning to Notre-Dame in a ceremony in December 2024.

An important material detail: what is preserved today is a ring of interwoven rushes, without any thorns. Scholars understand that the soldiers wove a kind of helmet of thorns, held together by this band of rushes; the sixty or seventy thorns had already been detached from the ring when the relic arrived in Paris, and were afterward distributed by Saint Louis and his successors as diplomatic gifts, none of which remains in Paris today. The earliest description of this object comes from the chronicler Robert de Clari, a participant in the Fourth Crusade, who describes it as the "blessed crown with which he was crowned, made of sea rushes, sharp as dagger blades." From the 13th century onward, the depiction of Christ crowned with thorns spread in Western art, becoming a central theme of Passion iconography.
