itens.resumo: The Latin cross encircled by a ring — the nimbus — at the point where the arms cross, typical of the great stone crosses of Ireland and Great Britain from the eighth century onward.
itens.corpo:
The Celtic cross — also called the ringed cross or, in English-speaking countries, the ringed cross — is characterized by a ring, the nimbus, that surrounds the point where the horizontal arms cross the vertical shaft. Its established form is that of the great monumental stone crosses (high crosses) erected in monasteries of Ireland and of the regions under Irish influence, above all between the eighth and twelfth centuries. These crosses were not gravestones, but monuments and landmarks: they marked the sacred precinct, served as places of preaching and prayer, and bore carved panels with scenes from the Old and New Testaments, intended for the instruction of the faithful.

Popular legend attributes the invention of the Celtic cross to Saint Patrick, who is said to have devised it by joining the Christian cross to the pagan symbol of the sun in order to ease the catechesis of the newly converted Celts. This account does not withstand chronology: the oldest known ringed crosses date from around 750-800, almost three centuries after the saint's death (c. 461). The examples at the monastery of Ahenny, in County Tipperary, made of sandstone in the eighth or ninth century, are among the oldest preserved and are notable for having almost no biblical figures: their faces and the ring are covered with spirals, interlacing (interlace), bosses and geometric patterns, at the height of the Celtic decorative tradition before the turn to figurative sculpture.

Regarding the origin of the ring, a technical hypothesis has gained strength in recent decades. The study of Saint John's Cross on Iona (the island of the monastery founded by Saint Columba, off the coast of Scotland) suggests that the ring did not originate as a symbolic element, but as an engineering solution: the head of the cross, with an exceptionally wide span, would have fallen and broken as early as the eighth century, and the four quadrants of the ring were added, in local stone, to prop up and reinforce the arms during the repair. An accident would thus have given rise to a fashion — and Saint John's Cross is today considered the progenitor of the ringed crosses, including the Irish examples of the ninth and tenth centuries. Symbolic readings of the ring also coexist: the supremacy of Christ over the sun venerated by pagan peoples, the Celtic idea of eternity without beginning or end, or the union between the cross (the Passion) and the circle (the Resurrection and the promise of eternal life).

Among the most famous crosses is Muiredach's Cross, at Monasterboice, in County Louth, dated to around 900-925 and considered by many scholars the most beautiful high cross in Ireland. It stands almost six meters tall, was carved from sandstone, and bears at its base an inscription generally translated as a prayer for Muiredach, the abbot for whom the cross was made — Muiredach mac Domhnaill, who died in 923 — flanked by two cats in relief, one of the most frequently cited details of medieval Irish sculpture. On the same site stands the West Cross, more slender and taller, also from the early tenth century, but much more eroded.

Over time, the ringed model became an identity symbol of Irish Christianity and of communities of Celtic origin throughout the world — reappearing with a different meaning in commemorative crosses in cemeteries and in modern goldsmithing, often as an emblem of cultural heritage rather than of devotion.

itens.resumo: The two central sacred vessels of the Mass, used to offer, consecrate, and receive Communion with the Eucharistic bread and wine.
itens.corpo:
The chalice is the cup in which the wine and a little water of the Eucharistic sacrifice are placed and, after the consecration, the Blood of Christ; the paten is the small plate, usually gilded and slightly concave, on which the bread to be consecrated is placed. The General Instruction of the Roman Missal expressly distinguishes them among the sacred vessels: they are those "intended for the offering, consecration, and reception of the bread and wine" (GIRM 327), which makes them the most central vessels of every celebration of the Mass.

The material and the form follow precise norms. Sacred vessels "should be made from noble metal"; if they are made of metal that rusts or of a metal less noble than gold, "they should ordinarily be gilded on the inside" (GIRM 328), and "the bowl of the chalice should be made of material that does not absorb liquids" (GIRM 330). With the confirmation of the Apostolic See, at the discretion of the Conferences of Bishops, ivory and "certain other woods that are solid and... very hard" are also permitted (GIRM 329). As for form, it is for the artist to give them the shape that best suits the customs of each region, provided it is suited to liturgical use (GIRM 295); and, before being destined exclusively for the Eucharist, the vessels receive a proper rite of blessing or consecration (GIRM 296; Book of Blessings, 1068-1073). This reserved character expresses before the community the distinction between the objects of divine worship and any profane use.

The legislation also regulates what goes on the altar. GIRM 293 recommends that, "for the consecration of the hosts, it is appropriate to use a single, larger paten, on which the bread is placed for the celebrant as well as for the ministers and the faithful." This provision partly recovers an ancient practice: in the first centuries the paten was a broad plate, used to collect the bread offered by the faithful and to distribute the consecrated fragments at Communion. When, around the ninth century, frequent Communion waned, "the use of the large and proportionally deep patinae ministeriales fell into disuse," and a much smaller paten became common, used exclusively by the priest at the altar, to hold the Host and prevent the scattering of particles. After Communion, the priest or the minister purifies the paten or the ciborium over the chalice, while saying quietly the prayer "What has passed our lips" (Quod ore sumpsimus), and wipes the chalice with the purificator (GIRM, Concluding Rites).

At the offertory, the preparation of the chalice is accompanied by a gesture of theological significance: a drop of water is poured into the wine. Tradition explains this mystery as the union of the divine nature and the human nature in Christ, and of the Church with her Lord, a theme that echoes in the prayer accompanying the gesture, "By the mystery of this water and wine..." (Deus, qui humanae substantiae). The water, which also represents humanity, is united to the wine, which represents Christ, to signify the people's intimate participation in the offering of the Eucharistic sacrifice.

The pair, chalice and paten, goes back to Christ's own gesture at the Last Supper, when he "took the bread and the cup"; for this reason the liturgical tradition treats them with the greatest material and symbolic care among the vessels of the altar.

itens.resumo: The covered sacred vessel — called a ciborium, pyx, or âmbula — used to keep the consecrated hosts in the tabernacle and to distribute them at the Communion of the faithful.
itens.corpo:
The ciborium, also called a pyx or (in Portuguese) âmbula, is the sacred vessel in the form of a chalice with a lid, intended to hold the consecrated hosts, both for the Communion of the assembly and for the Eucharistic reservation in the tabernacle. All three names are correct, but they prevailed in different periods: ciborium (from Medieval Latin ciborium, in turn from the Greek κιβώριον, kibórion, "drinking cup") was the most common term in past centuries; pyx comes from the Greek pyxís, "boxwood box," designating the small round box with a lid; âmbula, from the Latin ampulla, is linked to the idea of "carrying." Alongside the large tabernacle ciborium, it is common to distinguish a smaller pyx (or teca), used to bring Communion to the sick and the bedridden.

The name "ciborium" has, however, a second use that should not be confused with the first. In Christian architecture, a ciborium — in Portuguese also "baldaquino" (baldachin) — designates the canopy of stone or wood supported by columns and raised over the altar, common in early Christian and Romanesque basilicas; Bernini's famous bronze baldachin in Saint Peter's in the Vatican belongs to this family. The two meanings, that of the vessel and that of the canopy, derive from the same Greek word and coexist, which is why sources usually distinguish them explicitly.

Historically, the first ciboria were not intended for the church: in the ancient communities, the Eucharist was not habitually kept in places of worship, for fear of sacrilege or profanation, and the first containers were kept in private homes, at hand for the Communion of the sick and for Viaticum. When Eucharistic worship intensified — above all from the thirteenth century onward, with the institution of the feast of Corpus Christi (1246/1264) — the use of the ciborium with a lid for reservation in the tabernacle became established.

The use of this vessel is framed by precise canonical norms. The Code of Canon Law determines that the Most Holy Eucharist is to be habitually reserved in only one tabernacle of the church or oratory (can. 938 §1), located in a distinguished place, conspicuous, beautifully decorated, and suitable for prayer (can. 938 §2), immovable, made of solid and opaque material, and locked in such a way as to avoid the danger of profanation (can. 938 §3). It further prescribes that the consecrated hosts be kept "in a pyx or small vessel" in a quantity sufficient for the needs of the faithful, renewed frequently, with the older ones duly consumed (can. 939), and that a special lamp burn continuously before the tabernacle to indicate and honor the presence of Christ (can. 940).

Unlike the monstrance — a similar piece, also present in this collection, but intended to expose the Host for public adoration — the ciborium has the function of discreetly keeping and transporting the Eucharistic species, and for this reason it is fitted with a lid and is often covered with a veil. As for materials, the same criterion required of all vessels that receive the hosts applies to it: if the host is placed directly in the vessel, it must be made of noble metal or, at the very least, gilded on the inside (cf. GIRM 328-329).

itens.resumo: The Latin cross with a second, shorter arm above the larger one, used as an insignia of patriarchs and archbishops and indistinguishable in form from the Cross of Lorraine.
itens.corpo:
The patriarchal cross, also called the double cross or archiepiscopal cross, is a variant of the Latin cross that adds, above the main arm, a second, smaller arm closer to the top. The traditional reading associates this additional arm with the titulus crucis, the plaque that the Roman soldiers fixed above the head of Jesus with the inscription "INRI" (Iesus Nazarenus Rex Iudaeorum), so that the two arms together would recall both the cross of Christ and the title that accompanied it.

The oldest datable material record of the two-armed cross is numismatic: it appears regularly on Byzantine Empire coinage from the second reign of Emperor Justinian II (705–711), who is depicted on the solidus holding a globus cruciger topped by a patriarchal cross. The example is preserved, among other collections, in the Byzantine coin collection of Dumbarton Oaks. It is also recorded in the coinage and heraldry of the medieval West: Bishop Béla III of Hungary (1148–1196), who had lived in Constantinople, is said to have brought the two-armed cross into his shield, and it figures among the main elements of the arms of Hungary at least since around 1190, later passing to the arms of Lithuania (on the shield of the knight Vytis, in the Pahonia) and, between 1577 and 1625, to those of Russia, between the heads of the double-headed eagle. In medieval pilgrimage books, the patriarchal cross already served to mark the places where a plenary indulgence could be obtained, while the simple Latin cross indicated a partial indulgence.

Its adoption as an insignia of ecclesiastical dignity is what gives it its name: it distinguishes patriarchs and archbishops, in contrast to the single-armed pectoral cross used by bishops. In ecclesiastical heraldry, the two-armed archiepiscopal cross appears in the coat of arms of archbishops, alongside the green hat with ten tassels on each side; the pope, for his part, uses a three-armed cross. At the same time, the patriarchal cross is iconographically very frequent in Greco-Byzantine art and in the Eastern Orthodox Churches; in the Russian and Slavic version, a third short, slanted crossbar is sometimes added near the foot, which brings it close to the so-called Russian Orthodox cross.

The form of the patriarchal cross is practically identical to that of the Cross of Lorraine, and the two names are often used interchangeably. The Cross of Lorraine (Croix de Lorraine), also called the Cross of Anjou, figured in the symbolism of the Dukes of Anjou, who became Dukes of Lorraine from 1431; in the oldest version, the two arms were of the same size. René II of Lorraine (1451–1508) was the first to incorporate it as a symbol of the duchy, in opposition to the Cross of Burgundy, and tradition links it to the Battle of Nancy (January 5, 1477), in which he defeated Charles the Bold, Duke of Burgundy. In the twentieth century, the Cross of Lorraine was chosen by Émile Muselier, a vice-admiral of Lorraine origin, and adopted by Free France on July 1, 1940 as an emblem of resistance in opposition to the Nazi swastika, becoming a symbol of Gaullism. This double life — ecclesiastical insignia and political and national symbol — explains why the same two-armed cross appears both in the coat of arms of an archbishop and in the arms of Hungary, Lithuania or the former Slovakia.

itens.resumo: The white flower that accompanies images of Saint Joseph in Catholic iconography, a symbol of his purity and chastity, linked by pious tradition to the apocryphal account of the rod that blossomed.
itens.corpo:
In artistic representations of Saint Joseph, a white lily almost always appears in his hands — a symbol, in the Christian tradition, of purity of heart, of chastity, and also of the victory of life over death. The lily is so firmly established as the saint's attribute that it also appears in the hands of the Child Jesus when He is depicted in the arms of His adoptive father, and it serves as an emblem on coats of arms whose bearer has Saint Joseph as patron.

The origin of the flower is not found in the canonical Gospels, but in a set of apocryphal texts that popular piety brought together. In the Protoevangelium of James (2nd century), when Mary reaches the age of twelve, the priest Zechariah summons the widowers of the city so that each one may bring a rod, and a dove descends upon Joseph's rod, a sign that he had been chosen to take the Virgin under his protection; Joseph, feeling old and unworthy, at first refused, and only accepted after being rebuked by Zechariah to fear God more. In a later apocryphal work, the Gospel of Pseudo-Matthew's counterpart, the Gospel of the Nativity of Mary (5th century), the narrative changes: the candidates leave a dry branch on the altar, and Joseph's immediately blossoms, indicating the divine choice. The History of Joseph the Carpenter, probably from the 9th century, takes up the episode again: from Joseph's staff comes not a dove but a flower, and the Holy Spirit descends upon it. It was later popular piety that identified this flower as a lily. Classical iconography thus consolidated two associated images — the flowering rod and the white flower — which also derive from the prophecy of Isaiah (11:1) about the shoot that springs from the stump of Jesse, the lineage from which Joseph descends. Together, these accounts — seven apocryphal works in all mention Joseph — contributed, among other things, to representing him as an elderly man and a widower, a defense of the perpetual virginity of Mary against the groups that denied it.

This collection records the origin of the flower as legendary tradition, and not as historical fact, just as it distinguishes legend from Gospel narrative in other symbols gathered here, such as the Eucharistic pelican. Regardless of the legend, the lily became established as a fixed iconographic attribute of Saint Joseph, and Scripture provides symbolic foundations for the image: Christ himself, in the Sermon on the Mount, invites us to "consider the lilies of the field." The association with purity also explains the use of the lily in bridal bouquets and at wedding ceremonies.

The cult of Saint Joseph gained doctrinal momentum in the 19th century. On December 8, 1870, by means of the decree Quemadmodum Deus of the Sacred Congregation of Rites, Pope Pius IX solemnly proclaimed Saint Joseph Patron and Protector of the universal Church, raising the feast of March 19 to the rite of double of the first class. The coincidence of the date with the feast of the Immaculate Conception was deliberate, and the decree was promulgated while the First Vatican Council was in session, whose work had been suspended with the capture of Rome: the text compares Joseph, head of the Holy Family, to the one who received the charge of caring for "God's most precious treasures." In 1955, Pope Pius XII instituted the feast of Saint Joseph the Worker on May 1. Tradition also invokes him as patron of a happy death, according to the pious belief that he died in the presence of Jesus and Mary.
